name: The Cazneaux Tree

location.address: Ikara-Flinders Ranges National Park, west side of Flinders Ranges Way, ~3km north-east of Wilpena Pound Resort, South Australia

access: Free. Inside Ikara-Flinders Ranges National Park, reached via the Spirit of Endurance Trail (a 90-minute, Grade 2, no-experience-needed walking trail opened as an interpretive trail, easily accessible from Flinders Ranges Way). An SA National Parks entry pass may be required for vehicle entry to the park itself; the walk and the tree carry no separate fee.
transport: No public transport; self-drive via Flinders Ranges Way. Nearest services at Wilpena Pound Resort, ~3km away; nearest town Hawker is roughly 60km south.
verify_notes: Coordinates corroborated by two independent sources within about 150-200m of the brief's figure (Wikipedia infobox -31.520344/138.637187; brief -31.518867/138.6385), and the tree has its own interpretive sign and, since a Nov 2025 SA government post, a dedicated named walking trail built around it, so this is a genuine tree-level pin rather than a park-level guess. Species and measurements confirmed directly on Wikipedia, sourced to a 2018 SA government Location SA gazetteer citation: height 29m, circumference at the base 11.4m (girth_cm 1140). A separate, more recent SA government park blog (environment.sa.gov.au, published 27 Nov 2025, so very current and strong evidence the tree is alive today) instead gives a looser 'estimated to be around 25 metres tall' -- a rough approximation rather than a remeasurement, so the more specific historic 29m figure is used for height_m and the discrepancy is noted here rather than silently resolved. No age figure found anywhere for this specimen; age_estimate left as 'not documented' per the missing-age rule rather than guessed. History: a River Red Gum standing alone on an otherwise flat, arid grassland plateau, photographed in May 1937 by Harold Cazneaux (1878-1953, 'the father of Australian photography') during a camping trip with his wife and son; his image 'The Spirit of Endurance' brought him international recognition and the tree took its name from the photograph. Cazneaux's own words on it, quoted by the SA government in 1941: 'The passing of the years has left it scarred and marked by the elements - storm, fire, water - unconquered, it speaks to us of a Spirit of Endurance.' Named by the last pastoral leaseholder of Wilpena Station, George Hunt, per Cazneaux's daughter Rainbow Cazneaux. Listed as significant tree number 239 on the National Trust of South Australia's Register of Significant Trees, for 'its outstanding aesthetic beauty'. A plaque funded by Cazneaux's grandson, entrepreneur Dick Smith, was placed at the site in 1991. Single-tree-destination test: clearly passes -- subject of one of Australia's most reproduced photographs, National Trust registered, and now the anchor of its own purpose-built interpretive walking trail.
